meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'here, there', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Sit down right here and do not strain yourself.
Well there, something like that.

examples.text: Вот что ты ей хочешь сказать?
examples.trans: Now what do you want to say to her?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'so', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Well there, something like that.
So here is the deal.
What is the matter, Lyova? Easy.

meanings.note: Prefix 'вс-' ('up') marks upward or sudden onset of action (stem 'егда').

examples.text: Вот так, Аркадий, всегда набираешь вес.
examples.trans: Just like that, Arkady, you always gain weight.
She's always like that.
There's always a way out.

meanings.note: Prefix 'на-' marks surface contact, accumulation, or completing a quantity (stem 'бирать'). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'gain, put on', paired with 'набрать'.

examples.text: Вот так, Аркадий, всегда набираешь вес.
examples.trans: Just like that, Arkady, you always gain weight.
He is now gaining popularity.
The firm is recruiting new employees.

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'weight' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: Не знает ещё, как себя вести.
examples.trans: She does not know how to behave yet.

examples.text: Хочу немножко привести себя в порядок.
examples.trans: I want to get myself in shape a bit.

examples.text: Он весь день ест этот сельдерей.
examples.trans: He has been eating this celery all day.

meanings.note: Common neuter noun meaning 'champagne' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: Champagne for lovers? Apparently they mixed it up.
Open the champagne!
A glass of champagne, please.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'for', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Champagne for lovers? Apparently they mixed it up.
But for me you are not tasty.
We could open a salon for you.

meanings.note: Adjective formed with the common Slavic suffix '-н-' from a noun/verb root. Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('in love').

examples.trans: Champagne for lovers? Apparently they mixed it up.

examples.text: Я влюблён в неё с первого класса.
examples.trans: I've been in love with her since first grade.
She is in love with him.

meanings.note: Manner/predicative adverb in '-о', derived from the neuter short form of the corresponding adjective.

examples.text: Видишь, как опасно надо мной шутить!
examples.trans: See how dangerous it is to joke with me!
Champagne for lovers? Apparently they mixed it up.
But apparently I came in vain.

meanings.note: Prefix 'пере-' denotes crossing over, repeating, or exceeding a limit (stem 'путать'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'mixed up', paired with 'путать'.

examples.trans: Forgive me, I mixed everything up.
Champagne for lovers? Apparently they mixed it up.
Don't mix it up!

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'you (informal)', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: You have to tell me.
Did you chop the carrots?
Why do you not wear it?

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'think, suppose', paired with 'подумать'.

examples.text: Лёва, ты думаешь, я ничего не понимаю?
examples.trans: Lyova, do you think I do not understand anything?
Gulya? Do you think I would suit her?
I'm thinking about work.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'I', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Just as I assumed.
And why do I not know?
I do not owe you anything.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'nothing', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: I do not owe you anything.
What? I have not changed at all.

examples.text: Ну ничего, пиши. Девушки любят долго собираться.
examples.trans: Never mind, write. Girls love taking a long time to get ready.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'not', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: You have an incomplete rib fracture.
No. Stop it!
And why do I not know?

meanings.note: Prefix 'по-' forms perfective verbs or marks a brief/onset action (stem 'нимать'). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'understand', paired with 'понять'.

examples.text: Лёва, ты думаешь, я ничего не понимаю?
examples.trans: Lyova, do you think I do not understand anything?
I understand everything.
I understand.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'everything', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Заодно объясню, почему всё так вышло.
examples.trans: At the same time I will explain why it all happened this way.
Forgive me, I mixed everything up.

examples.text: Спасибо, Соломон Иванович. Теперь всё можно!
examples.trans: Thank you, Solomon Ivanovich. Now everything is allowed!

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'already', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Я уже три года вижу, как ты на меня смотришь.
examples.trans: For three years already I have seen how you look at me.

examples.text: Я уже четыре года работаю мэром.
examples.trans: I've been mayor for four years now.
Dad is already home.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian cardinal or ordinal numeral meaning 'three', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Whether anyone watches things here or not.

examples.text: Я уже три года вижу, как ты на меня смотришь.
examples.trans: For three years already I have seen how you look at me.
Three days.

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'years' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: She is working her first day today.

examples.text: Нет, спасибо. Я сегодня на диете.
examples.trans: No, thank you. I am on a diet today.
I am on a diet today!

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'see', paired with 'увидеть'.

examples.trans: Louis, did you not see them?

examples.text: Ты что, не видел, что я здесь стою?
examples.trans: Did you not see that I am standing here?

examples.text: Этого вообще никто не видел. Правда, Макс?
examples.trans: Nobody saw a thing at all. Right, Max?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'how', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Just as I assumed.
Be glad. How was the injury sustained?
Keep living just like before.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'on, onto', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: You said it was a crack.
Well, that is what it is.
Be glad. How was the injury sustained?

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'мотреть'). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'look, watch', paired with 'посмотреть'.

examples.trans: Look what I've got.
I'm watching TV.

examples.text: Привет! Смотри, что у меня есть.
examples.trans: Hi! Look what I've got.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'come on, well', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Well, that is what it is.
Well, I do not know.
Well why are you walking around?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'what, that', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Ты опять намекаешь, что я толстый?
examples.trans: Are you hinting again that I am fat?

examples.text: Нет, я просто говорю, что был стройный.
examples.trans: No, I am just saying that you were slim.
What is the matter, Lyova? Easy.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'such, what sort', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Well there, something like that.
So here is the deal.
What is the matter, Lyova? Easy.

meanings.note: Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('good').

examples.trans: Good news. Gulya agrees.

examples.text: Хорошо. Слушай, ну это деловая встреча.
examples.trans: Alright. Listen, well this is a business meeting.

examples.text: Ты такой хороший. Только не обижайся.
examples.trans: You are so good. Only do not take offense.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'only', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Only a wardrobe fell.
And I will speak only the truth.
I speak only the truth!

meanings.en: to take offence, to get upset
meanings.note: Prefix 'об-' ('around, about') marks encirclement or comprehensive action (stem 'ижаться'). Reflexive/intransitive verb with the postfix '-ся'/'-сь' (historically from the reflexive pronoun 'себя', oneself). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'take offense', paired with 'обидеться'.

examples.trans: Don't take offence, Vanya.
Don't be offended by my words.

examples.text: Да не обижайся ты, Ваня. Сейчас найду подходящую одежду.
examples.trans: Don't take offence, Vanya. I'll find suitable clothes right now.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian clause-linking conjunction meaning 'but', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Why do you not wear it?
I am telling you for sure!
What is the matter, Lyova? Easy.

meanings.note: Negative prefix 'не-' ('un-, non-, not') (stem 'вкусный'). Adjective formed with the common Slavic suffix '-н-' from a noun/verb root. Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('not tasty').

examples.trans: But for me you are not tasty.

examples.text: Шеф говорит, что это очень невкусный выбор.
examples.trans: The chef says that this is a very not tasty choice.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'in, into', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Go have breakfast later.
You have an incomplete rib fracture.
You said it was a crack.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'my', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Елена Павловна нашла мой старый костюм.
examples.trans: Elena Pavlovna found my old suit.

examples.text: Ладно, пачкай тарелки, потом иди мой.
examples.trans: Alright, dirty the plates, then go wash them.
You, me, and my suit.

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'taste, type' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: But for me you are not tasty.

examples.text: Ну, не в моём вкусе ты.
examples.trans: Well, you are not my type.
You are not my type.

meanings.note: Derived noun with agent/object suffix '-ник'/'-щик'/'-чик'. Common feminine noun meaning 'niece' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: She is my niece.

examples.text: Вот моей племяннице подошёл бы, Гульнаре.
examples.trans: Now you would suit my niece, Gulnara.
My favorite niece.

meanings.en: to come up to, to approach
meanings.note: Prefix 'под-' ('under, up to') indicates approaching or supporting from below (stem 'ойти'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to come up (to), to approach', paired with 'подходить'.

examples.trans: Come here to me!
Keep away from my child!

examples.text: Нам не нужна ваша приставка! Ещё раз подойдёте к моему ребёнку — пожалеете!
examples.trans: We don't need your console! Come near my child again and you'll be sorry!

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'would', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Be glad. How was the injury sustained?
Quickly back to work, Lavrov!
Listen, how slim you used to be!

meanings.note: Manner/predicative adverb in '-о', derived from the neuter short form of the corresponding adjective.

examples.trans: Of course! Let us have a drink.
Goodness, well of course not!
Of course I'll help.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'come on', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

related.gloss: to give (the verb it comes from)

examples.text: Давай я помогу. Хочешь пригласить её на свидание?
examples.trans: Let me help. Do you want to invite her on a date?
Vika, let me drive it over.
Let me help you, huh?

meanings.en: to drink up, to have a drink
meanings.note: Prefix 'вы-' ('out of') marks outward movement or thorough completion (stem 'пить'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'let's drink', paired with 'выпивать'.

examples.text: Какое совпадение! А у меня есть желание выпить.
examples.trans: What a coincidence! And I have a desire to drink.
Oh, I've had a bit to drink now.
Drink some water.
